title: What is known about 1RB0RA_1LC0RA_0LF0LD_1LE---_0LC0LB_1LA0RE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RA_1LC0RA_0LF0LD_1LE---_0LC0LB_1LA0RE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a sweep counter: each sweep adds a 1 to the youngest block and moves a one or two 1s between older blocks at a place fixed by the binary digits of the sweep number. Lean proves ten whole-sweep rules for every block length (the generic parity patterns), and that the run from blank tape reaches such a sweep; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 1.03·1011 steps (226,517 sweeps).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: B with 1 two left, 1 left, 0 under the head; E with 1 two left, 1 left, 0 under the head. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Ten whole-sweep rules
claims.text: With block counts written last block first, a sweep from B>0 at the right end back to it changes them by: (E | O ?) → (+1, +1, −1); (E | E E ?) → (+1, −1, +2, −1); (E | E O E ?) → (+1, −1, 0, +2, −1); (O | E E E ?) and (O | E O O E) → (+1, 0, 0, +1, −1); (O | E E O E E) → (+1, 0, 0, −1, +2, −1), where E/O is the parity of a count (inner counts at least 4, the last at least 5), for every value of the counts and every tape further left; the step counts are linear (e.g. 8c + 16y1 + 76 for the first). Written by bbtools.symtm.prove.

claims.title: From blank tape to a generic sweep
claims.text: After 2,183 steps the tape is (10)^27 0 (10)^12 0 (10)^4 0 (10)^9 1 B>0 (counts 27, 12, 4, 10), and the next sweep is the rule sweep_E_EEO, ending at step 2,367 as the simulator says.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.03·10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: c/sweeps.c (a plain simulator that also counts sweeps) runs 1.03·1011 steps, 226,517 sweeps, without a halt. The sweeps that reach the leftmost 1 of the tape (the only ones that add new blocks there) are rare: 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 16, 32, 48, 64, 160, 192, 448, 1472, 1984, 2496, 3008, 3520, 11712, 28096, 60864 and 126400 (none more up to sweep 226,517).

claims.title: The sweep number is a binary counter
claims.text: In the 31,158 sweeps of the first 2·109 steps, every sweep adds 1 to the last block and, except a handful where the number of blocks changes, makes exactly one more change: a move Mk (block 2k+1 gains a 1, block 2k+2 loses one; blocks counted from the last, which is block 0) or a split Sk,j (block 2k+1 loses one, a block j places further left gains two, the next one loses one). The level k is the number of trailing zeros of the sweep number n in binary (n odd: k = 0; n = 2 mod 4: k = 1; ...), and M or S follows n mod 2k+2 and the parities of the blocks further left. Frequencies halve with each level, like the carries of a binary counter.
claims.where: computed from tmrun ... at B R snapshots (see README)

claims.title: Regular-language deciders tried (F11)
claims.text: None of these closes: each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction, which says nothing about whether the machine halts. n-gram CPS (tools/c/ngramcps.c), equal widths on both sides: a halting local configuration is reached with plain up to width 24, history 1 up to width 20, history 2 up to width 24, history 3 up to width 22, LRU history up to width 22 (larger widths ran out of the 150 s or 60 million configuration budget). n-gram CPS with every cell tagged by its position mod p: fails for p = 2 up to width 20, p = 3 up to width 20, p = 4 up to width 20, p = 6 up to width 20. n-gram CPS where each side also carries the state of a small automaton that has read that side from the far end (every automaton with up to 3 states on both sides, or 4 states on one side), with position mod 1..4 and widths 4, 6, 8: no closed set without a halt in all 120 parameter sets. Run-length windows (the K nearest runs of equal macro cells on each side, run lengths kept exactly below T and mod M above): fails for all 72 parameter sets (cells of 1 to 4 bits, K = 2, 4, 6, T = 2, 4, M = 1, 2, 4). Two-automaton closed tape language by SAT (a deterministic automaton reading each side inward, n states each, CaDiCaL): no solution for n = 2..7; n = 8 not finished in 150 s.
claims.where: sweeps of 13 November 2026 (family F11); the tagged and run-length deciders are not in the repository yet

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: The only halting transition is D reading 1: the left-moving head (C, D, E, B rotating over the 10s) meeting two adjacent 1s. None of the generic sweep rules does that; whether a sweep over short blocks (counts below 4, the empty blocks that sometimes appear) or the arrival of a carry at the left end can do it is not settled.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB---_0RC0RF_0RD0RA_1RE0LB_1LF0LE_1RC0LE up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is a row of blocks of 10s. Each sweep adds a 1 to the newest block, which therefore counts the sweeps, and makes one small change further back, at a place chosen by the binary digits of the sweep number: the old blocks behave like the digits of a binary counter. Lean proves the sweep rules for the common block patterns; the simulator finds no halt in 1.03·10<sup>11</sup> steps.

facts.text: Whole sweeps for every block length, proved in Lean.
No halt in the C simulator (226,517 sweeps).
Where the sweep makes its change, read off the sweep number n.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.527).
After 109 steps the tape spans 44,255 cells (419 left of the start, 31,877 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: What the tape is made of
html: Almost every cell pair on the tape is 10. The exceptions are single extra 0s, which cut the tape into blocks of 10s. Count the 1s in each block: right after a sweep the tape reads, for example, 4, 3, 26, 13, 3, 24. The last (rightmost) block is special: it gains exactly one 1 per sweep, so it simply counts the sweeps.

The head never stays long anywhere: in state C it runs left over 10s shifting each 1 one cell left (four steps per two 1s), in A/B it runs right shifting them back; inside the region it is working on it zigzags, crossing a 1010 in 12 steps.

sections.heading: One sweep, in numbers
html: A sweep starts with the head in state B on the blank cell right of the tape, runs left over the last block, works its way further left through a few blocks, and comes back. What it does depends only on the parities of the block counts it meets (E even, O odd), read from the right. Writing the counts last block first:

parities (last | inner …)change of the countssteps
E | O ?+1, +1, −18c + 16y1 + 76
E | E E ?+1, −1, +2, −18c + 16y1 + 16y2 + 104
E | E O E ?+1, −1, 0, +2, −18c + 16(y1+y2+y3) + 148
O | E E E ?+1, 0, 0, +1, −18c + 16y1 + 32y2 + 16y3 + 168
O | E E O E E+1, 0, 0, −1, +2, −18c + 16y1 + 32y2 + 16y3 + 16y4 + 212

(c, yi: a count is 2y+4 or 2y+5, the last 2c+5 or 2c+6.) These are proved in Lean for every value of the counts. Deeper patterns behave the same way: always one move of a single 1 to the right neighbour, or a split where a block takes one 1 from each side (sometimes skipping a few odd blocks).

sections.heading: A binary counter made of block pairs
html: Which block a sweep changes is decided by the sweep number n, the length of the last block. In the first 31,158 sweeps (2·109 steps) it was, with a handful of exceptions where the number of blocks changes:

sweep numberchange (blocks counted from the last = 0)
n ≡ 1 (mod 4)M0: block 1 +1, block 2 −1
n ≡ 3 (mod 4)S0,j: block 1 −1, block 2+j +2, block 3+j −1
n ≡ 2 (mod 4)M1 or S1,j (blocks 3, 4 and beyond)
n ≡ 4 (mod 8)M2 or S2,j (blocks 5, 6 and beyond)
n = 2k · oddMk or Sk,j (blocks 2k+1, 2k+2 and beyond)

So blocks 1 and 2 are the units digit of a binary counter, blocks 3 and 4 the twos digit, and so on: the pair 2k+1, 2k+2 is touched only by sweeps whose number has exactly k trailing zeros, half as often as the pair before. A split S also passes a 1 further left, like a carry. When a carry reaches the left end, a few new blocks of 3s and 4s appear there; that happened at sweeps 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 16, 32, 48, 64, 160, 192, 448, 1472, 1984, 2496, 3008, 3520, 11712, 28096, 60864 and 126400 (none more up to sweep 226,517).

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The only missing transition is D reading 1. D is entered when C, running left, erases a 1; it halts if the next cell to the left is a 1 too. Over runs of 10s that never happens, and none of the sweep rules does it. A halt would need a sweep over very short blocks (counts below 4, including the empty blocks that sometimes form between two extra 0s) or the arrival of a carry at the left end to produce two adjacent 1s in front of C. Nobody has shown that this cannot happen, and the closed-tape-language method fails on this machine for every window up to 6.

sections.heading: What is proved
html: Lean (kernel): ten whole-sweep rules for all block lengths (lean/Rules.lean). Lean (native_decide): from blank tape the machine reaches the sweep start with counts 27, 12, 4, 10 after 2,183 steps, and the next sweep is one of the rules (lean/Reach.lean); no halt in the first 107 steps (lean/Blank.lean). Computed: no halt in 1.03·1011 steps. Open: a proof that the binary-counter picture holds for every sweep, and that short blocks and the left end never produce a halt.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: binary counter of block pairs (sweep counter)
summary: The tape is a row of blocks of 10s; every sweep adds one 1 to the last block (a sweep counter n) and makes one small change further left whose place is set by the binary digits of n, like a binary counter whose digits are pairs of blocks; open.
